name: Respect Yourself
description: “Respect Yourself” is a 1971 single by the Staple Singers, released October 1, 1971, on Stax Records and written by Luther Ingram and Mack Rice, produced by Al Bell with the Muscle Shoals Rhythm Section and the Memphis Horns. The song carried the Staples' gospel-rooted family harmonies into an explicit message of self-respect and mutual regard at the height of the civil rights era's cultural turn. It reached number 12 on the Billboard Hot 100 and number 2 on the Hot Soul Singles chart, becoming the group's breakthrough pop hit and the title track of their 1972 album Be Altitude: Respect Yourself. The recording was inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame in 2002 and appears on Rolling Stone's 500 Greatest Songs list. The song is staged as its own record, distinct from the album record already in the graph, on the same song-versus-album precedent applied in Wave 1.

name: Roberta Martin
description: Roberta Martin was a Chicago gospel singer, pianist, and songwriter who led the Roberta Martin Singers and stands, in CTL's gospel research, as the ensemble-and-training pipeline of Chicago gospel in one career. She worked as pianist at Ebenezer Baptist Church alongside Thomas A. Dorsey and Theodore Frye — a provenance documented in the Smithsonian's archival finding aid for the Roberta Martin collection. In 1933 she organized the Martin-Frye Quartet, which became the Roberta Martin Singers in 1936; women members including Bessie Folk and Delois Barrett Campbell joined in the mid-1940s, documenting women's centrality to a flagship gospel ensemble. CTL's gospel brief places her inside the networked system — Dorsey's composing, Frye's chorus direction, Ebenezer's institutional base — that carried Chicago gospel from storefront and Holiness churches into mainline congregations and national circulation in the 1930s and 1940s. The graph record's era for her work is the 1940s–1960s, and her sources include the Gospel Music Hall of Fame.

description: Robin Robinson (born Robin Carolle Robinson, August 4, 1957, in Chicago, Illinois) is an American television news anchor and radio host best known for a 27-year run as a main anchor at Fox-owned WFLD-TV (FOX 32) in Chicago. The daughter of Louie Robinson, West Coast editor of Ebony magazine, and Mati Robinson, she moved with her family to Pomona, California, in 1960 and to Claremont in 1963, where she helped integrate Claremont High School. She earned a bachelor's degree in journalism from San Diego State University, began her career in 1979 at KGTV in San Diego, and worked at KMGH in Denver before joining Chicago's WBBM-TV in 1984 as a consumer reporter and then anchor. In 1987 she joined WFLD as part of its first evening news team, co-anchoring for years with Walter Jacobson and later Bob Sirott and winning local Emmy Awards. She stepped down from the 9 p.m. anchor desk in November 2013, left WFLD on July 28, 2014, and moved to radio — fill-in anchor at WBBM (AM) from April 2015 and host of Robin's Nest on WVON from May 2015.

name: Richard Hunt
description: Richard Howard Hunt was an American sculptor born September 12, 1935, on Chicago's South Side. He began youth classes at the Art Institute of Chicago at thirteen and received his B.A.E. from the School of the Art Institute of Chicago in 1957, developing the direct-welding technique in salvaged and new metal for which he became known. His Hero Construction (1958) entered the Art Institute's collection within a year of his graduation. In 1971 he became the first African American sculptor to receive a retrospective at the Museum of Modern Art in New York. Working largely in abstract welded metal on themes of flight, uplift, and emancipation, he completed more large-scale public commissions than any other American sculptor; his Chicago works include Jacob's Ladder (1977) at the Carter G. Woodson Library, Flight Forms (2002) at Midway Airport, and The Light of Truth Ida B. Wells National Monument (2021) in Bronzeville, and his Swing Low (2016) hangs in the Smithsonian's National Museum of African American History and Culture. He served on the governing board of the National Endowment for the Arts. Hunt died December 16, 2023, in Chicago, aged 88.

name: Romare Bearden
aliases: Romare Howard Bearden; Romare H. Bearden
description: Romare Bearden was an American artist celebrated for paintings and collages drawn from African American life in the South, Pittsburgh, and Harlem. Born in Charlotte, North Carolina, he grew up mainly in Harlem, where his family's apartment drew writers, artists, and jazz musicians of the Harlem Renaissance. He graduated from New York University in 1935, studied at the Art Students League under George Grosz, and worked for much of his life as a New York City social-services caseworker while making art. After Army service and study in Paris on the G.I. Bill, he returned to New York. In 1963 he helped form Spiral, a collective of Black artists considering art's role in the civil rights movement, and his 1964 Projections exhibition of photomontage-based works brought him wide recognition; by 1966 he could support himself as an artist. Jazz and blues rhythms shaped his collage practice, and he also wrote on art. He received the National Medal of Arts a year before his death in New York in 1988.

name: Rihanna
description: Rihanna, born Robyn Rihanna Fenty on February 20, 1988, in Saint Michael, Barbados, and raised in Bridgetown, is a Barbadian singer, actress, and businesswoman whose career redefined the scale of a pop star from the Caribbean. Discovered in Barbados by producer Evan Rogers in 2003, she recorded demos in the United States and, after auditioning in early 2005 for Jay-Z, then president of Def Jam Recordings, signed with the label the same day. Her Caribbean-influenced debut Music of the Sun (2005) and A Girl Like Me (2006) reached the Billboard 200 top ten, before Good Girl Gone Bad (2007) and its single 'Umbrella' made her a global star and brought her first Grammy Award. Through Rated R (2009), Loud (2010), Talk That Talk (2011), and Unapologetic (2012), her first Billboard 200 number one, she sustained a run of chart-topping singles, then asserted greater creative control on Anti (2016), her second number-one album. Since 2016 she has released no new studio album, focusing on her Fenty Beauty and Savage X Fenty businesses, film roles, philanthropy through the Clara Lionel Foundation, and a celebrated Super Bowl LVII halftime performance in 2023.
